models.sample_description: U.S.-incorporated Compustat firm-year sample, 1995–2007, with assets of at least $10 million and nonmissing CIK; tax expense/income inputs and pretax income components are required subject to the source’s Table 2 missing-value rules. Multinational firms have nonzero TXFO or PIFO and are linked to material foreign operations using Form 10-K Exhibit 21. Parent pool: 15,231 firm-years and 3,433 unique firms. The two reported sign-stratum Ns are 10,285 for PI > 0 and 4,304 for PI ≤ 0; the table reports nonzero-weight observations for each separate robust-regression fit.
models.method_details: The authors state that all tables use robust regression to control for outliers. They describe iterative observation weights; zero-weight observations are excluded. The exact robust-regression routine, weight function and tuning choices are not identified.

dependent_variable.name: TXWW
dependent_variable.definition: Current worldwide tax expense, defined by the authors as Compustat TXT minus TXDI, scaled by total assets. If TXWW is missing while TXFED and TXFO are observed, the source sets TXWW = TXFED + TXFO.
dependent_variable.formula: (TXT − TXDI) / AT; if missing and TXFED and TXFO are observed, TXWW = TXFED + TXFO.

evidence.quote: TXWW is current worldwide tax expense (TXT-TXDI).
TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If TXWW is missing and TXFED and TXFO are not missing, then we set TXWW to TXFED + TXFO.

independent_variables.name: PI × HAVENYEAR
independent_variables.definition: Product of PI (Worldwide pretax income (Compustat PI), scaled by total assets. The source imputes PI as PIDOM + PIFO when PI is missing and both components are available.) and HAVENYEAR (Indicator equal to one if the firm reported at least one material operation in a country classified as a tax haven in year t, and zero otherwise. The static haven list classifies countries identified by at least three of four cited sources as of March 4, 2008.). The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimating the interaction model; this product is formed from the specified terms, with only continuous components subject to that centering.

evidence.quote: TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If PI is missing and PIFO and PIDOM are not missing, then we set PI to PIDOM + PIFO.
Using these data, we set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise.
We consider a country to be a tax haven if it was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008.
HAVENYEAR indicates at least one material operation in a tax haven country in year t listed in the firm’s form 10-K, exhibit 21. Tax haven countries are identified as in table 1.

weights.description: Robust regression iteratively assigns weights to reduce the influence of outliers. Observations with weight 0 are omitted; reported table Ns count observations with nonzero weights. The weight function and tuning choices are not reported.

estimation_procedure.description: The authors fit the same specification separately by pretax-income sign strata because the income-tax relation is treated as piecewise with a kink at zero. Table 3 partitions by PI; Tables 4–6 partition jointly by PIDOM and PIFO signs. Robust-regression table Ns count nonzero-weight observations, not the total parent sample.

evidence.quote: We believe that tax rates are nonlinear in pretax income with most of the change in slope occurring at 0 pretax income.
The first column estimates the model for firm-years with positive pretax income only ( PI > 0). The second column estimates the model for firm-years with negative pretax income only ( PI ≤ 0).
We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

preprocessing.description: The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimation to facilitate interpretation of interaction effects. The reference sample used to calculate means is not stated.

evidence.quote: We subtract the mean of all continuous variables to facilitate the interpretation of the coefficients.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.
Selected coefficient estimates from equations (9) and (10) are presented in table 8.

method.quote: We use robust regression to control for outliers in all tables.
robust regression iteratively assigns weights to observations to mitigate the
influence of outliers, some observations effectively receive a weight of 0, and are not included in the regression.

equation.quote: The model in equation (7) constrains the coefficient on PIit to be the same for domestic and foreign pretax incomes.
We estimate this model in table 3.
TXWW it = γ 0 + γ 1 P Iit + γ 2 P Iit ∗ HAVENYEAR it
In this table, we report estimates obtained from equation (7):

All variables</sup> are defined in table 2

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.
The first column estimates the model for firm-years with positive pretax income only ( PI > 0). The second column estimates the model for firm-years with negative pretax income only ( PI ≤ 0).

dependencies.quote: we use a regression framework to identify the variation in tax expense measures associated with income earned in different locations.

missing_fields.sample_size: The selected family comprises two separate sign-stratum fits with different reported Ns (10,285 and 4,304), so no single per-fit N applies to this grouped model record; sample_size is null and both exact Ns are retained in sample_description.
missing_fields.sample_description: The multinational classification uses nonzero TXFO or PIFO. The paper’s printed TXFO imputation rule 9 is self-referential, so the intended value for affected missing-TXFO observations—and any resulting effect on sample classification—cannot be established from the source.
missing_fields.specifications.preprocessing: The paper says all continuous variables are mean-centered but does not state whether the reference mean is computed in the full sample or separately within the sign-stratum fits.

review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

In the first column we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pre-tax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.

estimation_procedure.description: The authors fit the same specification separately by pretax-income sign strata because the income-tax relation is treated as piecewise with a kink at zero. Table 3 partitions by PI; Tables 4–6 partition jointly by PIDOM and PIFO signs. Robust-regression table Ns count nonzero-weight observations, not the total parent sample.

evidence.quote: We believe that tax rates are nonlinear in pretax income with most of the change in slope occurring at 0 pretax income.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported

The static haven list classifies countries identified by at least three of four cited sources as of March 4, 2008.). The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimating the interaction model; this product is formed from the specified terms, with only continuous components subject to that centering.

evidence.quote: TXFED, TXFO, TXWW , PIDOM, PIFO, PI, XAD, XRD, and DLTT are scaled by total assets (AT).
If PIFO is missing and PIDOM is equal to PI, then we set PIFO to 0.

Using these data, we set the variable HAVENYEAR equal to 1 if the firm has operations in at least one tax haven country in year t, 0 otherwise.
We consider a country to be a tax haven if it was identified as a haven by at least three of four sources as reported at http://www.globalpolicy.org on March 4, 2008.
HAVENYEAR indicates at least one material operation in a tax haven country in year t listed in the firm’s form 10-K, exhibit 21. Tax haven countries are identified as in table 1.

models.equation_text: TXFO_it = a0 + θ1 PIDOM_it + φ1 PIFO_it + θ2 (PIDOM_it × HAVENYEAR_it) + φ2 (PIFO_it × HAVENYEAR_it) + Σ_k θk (PIDOM_it × CONTROL^k_it) + Σ_k φk (PIFO_it × CONTROL^k_it) + u_it, where CONTROL^k is each of HAVENFIRM, NOL, LNAT, DLTT, XAD, and XRD. The fit is estimated separately for the four PIDOM/PIFO sign combinations.

fixed_effects.details: The paper does not report a fixed-effects structure for these fits. The equation and tables list regressors but do not explicitly state that fixed effects are absent.

standard_errors.details: Multiway clustered standard errors by firm and year (separate clustering dimensions).

evidence.quote: Standard errors are reported below the coefficient estimates in parenthesis, and are clustered by firm and year.
In this table, we report estimates obtained from equation (8)

weights.description: Robust regression iteratively assigns weights to reduce the influence of outliers. Observations with weight 0 are omitted; reported table Ns count observations with nonzero weights. The weight function and tuning choices are not reported.

evidence.quote: We use robust regression to control for outliers in all tables.
robust regression iteratively assigns weights to observations to mitigate the
influence of outliers, some observations effectively receive a weight of 0, and are not included in the regression.
We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

estimation_procedure.description: The authors fit the same specification separately by pretax-income sign strata because the income-tax relation is treated as piecewise with a kink at zero. Table 3 partitions by PI; Tables 4–6 partition jointly by PIDOM and PIFO signs. Robust-regression table Ns count nonzero-weight observations, not the total parent sample.

evidence.quote: We believe that tax rates are nonlinear in pretax income with most of the change in slope occurring at 0 pretax income.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported
We report the number of observations with nonzero weights in the N for each regression, which accounts for the slightly varying N from table to table.

preprocessing.description: The authors subtract the mean of all continuous variables before estimation to facilitate interpretation of interaction effects. The reference sample used to calculate means is not stated.

evidence.quote: We subtract the mean of all continuous variables to facilitate the interpretation of the coefficients.

scope.quote: We address two primary research questions in this study. First, do firms with material operations in tax haven countries face lower current tax rates than other firms? Second, do firms with material operations in any of 99 countries face higher or lower current tax rates than firms without operations in a particular country?

We use a new research methodology coupled with public financial accounting data to compute worldwide, federal, and foreign current tax rates on worldwide, domestic, and foreign income in order to examine these questions.
Selected coefficient estimates from equations (9) and (10) are presented in table 8.
We estimate equation (8) with the dependent variable changed to TXFO in table 6.

method.quote: We use robust regression to control for outliers in all tables.
robust regression iteratively assigns weights to observations to mitigate the
influence of outliers, some observations effectively receive a weight of 0, and are not included in the regression.

equation.quote: We estimate equation (8) with the dependent variable changed to TXFO in table 6.
TXFOit = a 0 + θ 1 PIDOM it + φ 1 PIFOit + θ 2 PIDOM it ∗ HAVENYEAR it + φ 2 PIFOit ∗ HAVENYEAR it

sample.quote: Our sample consists of all U.S. incorporated firms in the Compustat database between 1995 and 2007 that have at least $10 million in total assets (TA) and a nonmissing CIK number (CIK) so we can link the firm to data from the Securities and Exchange Commission Web site.
We require firms to have nonmissing values of worldwide current tax expense (TXT−TXDI), federal current tax expense (TXFED), and foreign current tax expense (TXFO).

Visual inspection of several form 10-K filings reveals that many of the missing values for these variables in Compustat should be coded as 0. Thus, to increase our sample size, we replace missing values as follows:
We define a firm as multinational if it has a nonzero value of foreign current tax expense ( TXFO ) or pretax foreign income ( PIFO ).
We match each Compustat firm-year to a data set gathered from each firm-year’s exhibit 21 of form 10-K filed on the Securities and Exchange Commission web page at www.sec.gov.
Imposing these requirements on the data translates into a sample of 15,231 firm- years corresponding to 3,433 unique firms.
If TXFO is missing and TXFED and TXWW are not missing, we set TXFO to TXWW −TXFO.

In the first column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the second column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with positive domestic pretax income ( PIDOM > 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). In the third column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and positive foreign pretax income ( PIFO > 0). In the fourth column, we report estimates for the subset of firm-years with negative domestic pretax income ( PIDOM ≤ 0) and negative foreign pretax income ( PIFO ≤ 0). Standard errors are reported

dependencies.quote: we use a regression framework to identify the variation in tax expense measures associated with income earned in different locations.

missing_fields.sample_size: The selected family comprises four sign-stratum fits with different reported Ns (6,728 2,312 2,387 2,486), so no single per-fit N applies to this grouped model record; sample_size is null and exact group Ns are retained in sample_description.
missing_fields.sample_description: The multinational classification uses nonzero TXFO or PIFO. The paper’s printed TXFO imputation rule 9 is self-referential, so the intended value for affected missing-TXFO observations—and any resulting effect on sample classification—cannot be established from the source.
missing_fields.specifications.preprocessing: The paper says all continuous variables are mean-centered but does not state whether the reference mean is computed in the full sample or separately within the sign-stratum fits.
missing_fields.dependent_variable.definition: The source’s TXFO definition is clear as current foreign tax expense scaled by assets, but its printed rule 9 assigns TXFO = TXWW − TXFO when TXFO is missing. The intended right-hand value cannot be established and is retained unresolved.

review_notes: The source prints a self-referential TXFO missing-value rule (TXFO = TXWW − TXFO); its intended value is unresolved. Because the multinational sample definition also uses TXFO, this may affect sample classification. No correction is inferred.
